what_its_for: Blinatumomab is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of blood cancer called B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It works by helping your immune system find and destroy cancer cells. It is used in adults and children, including those whose cancer has come back or has not responded to other treatments.
how_to_take: Blinatumomab is NOT a pill. It is given as a slow, continuous drip through an IV (intravenous) line into your vein. You will receive it at a hospital, infusion center, or sometimes at home with a special pump. The medicine runs continuously 24 hours a day for several days at a time. A healthcare provider will set up and monitor your infusion. Do not adjust the pump or IV line yourself. Make sure you understand how to care for your IV line at home if you are sent home with the infusion pump.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your body size (height and weight), your age, and your specific condition. Treatment is given in cycles. A typical cycle lasts about 4 to 6 weeks, which includes several weeks of continuous infusion followed by a rest period. You may need more than one cycle. Children and adults may receive different doses. Always follow your care team's specific instructions for your treatment schedule.
missed_dose: Because this medicine runs continuously through an IV pump, it is very important that it is never interrupted or stopped without your doctor's knowledge. If your infusion stops for any reason — such as a disconnected line, an empty bag, or a pump alarm — contact your healthcare team or go to the infusion center right away. Do not restart the pump on your own without guidance. Your doctor may need to restart your treatment at a lower dose if it was stopped for more than 4 hours.
storage: Your healthcare team will prepare and store the medicine for you. The prepared solution in the IV bag should be stored in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F or 2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it away from direct light. The IV bag can hang at room temperature during your infusion. Your care team will tell you exactly how long each bag is good for and when it needs to be replaced. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require full mental alertness, especially at the start of treatment, because this medicine can cause confusion, dizziness, or seizures. Avoid contact with people who are sick, since your immune system may be weakened. Do not get live vaccines while on this treatment without talking to your doctor first. Avoid drinking alcohol without checking with your doctor. Tell all of your healthcare providers (including dentists) that you are receiving this medicine before any procedure.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: high fever, chills, or signs of infection; confusion, trouble speaking, memory problems, loss of balance, or seizures; severe headache; chest pain or fast heartbeat; shortness of breath; swelling of the face, lips, or throat; severe skin rash or redness; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine; unusual bleeding or bruising; or if your IV line becomes disconnected or you are unsure if the pump is working properly. These can be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Your doctor will monitor your response to treatment with regular blood tests and check-ups. Some patients may begin to see improvement within the first one or two treatment cycles, but it can vary from person to person. Do not stop treatment early even if you are feeling better, unless your doctor tells you to. Keep all of your scheduled appointments so your care team can track how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Children: Blinatumomab is approved for use in children and doses are carefully adjusted based on body size. Children need close monitoring throughout treatment. Pregnant women: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 48 hours after the last dose. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 48 hours after the last dose, as it is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Older adults: Older patients may have a higher risk of certain side effects such as confusion and should be monitored closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how you respond to treatment.
